articles.title: The Prophet's Marriages: Zaynab, Ṣafiyyah and Māriyah
articles.excerpt: Critics present three of the Prophet's marriages as evidence of lust and exploitation. The sources tell a more complicated story, and the Quran addresses one of them directly.
articles.content:
After the age of Aisha, three relationships in the Prophet's life attract the most criticism. Zaynab bint Jaḥsh had been married to his adopted son Zayd. Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy was a captive after the conquest of Khaybar. Māriyah the Copt came to Medina as a gift from the ruler of Egypt. The prophet's marriages, critics argue, show a man who took what he wanted and produced revelations to justify it. Each case rests on specific sources, and each deserves to be examined on them.

[ce_figure id="pexels-11259857"]The iconic Green Dome of Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina, Saudi Arabia, with surrounding minarets.[/ce_figure]

Zaynab bint Jaḥsh and the adopted son

Zayd ibn Ḥārithah had been a slave in the Prophet's household, freed and adopted by him before the prophethood, and known as Zayd ibn Muḥammad. The Prophet arranged his marriage to Zaynab, his own cousin, a woman of noble lineage who accepted the match reluctantly. The marriage was unhappy, and Zayd came repeatedly to the Prophet wanting to divorce her. The Quran records what followed:

وَإِذْ تَقُولُ لِلَّذِىٓ أَنْعَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَأَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِ أَمْسِكْ عَلَيْكَ زَوْجَكَ وَٱتَّقِ ٱللَّهَ وَتُخْفِى فِى نَفْسِكَ مَا ٱللَّهُ مُبْدِيهِ وَتَخْشَى ٱلنَّاسَ وَٱللَّهُ أَحَقُّ أَن تَخْشَىٰهُ ۖ فَلَمَّا قَضَىٰ زَيْدٌۭ مِّنْهَا وَطَرًۭا زَوَّجْنَٰكَهَا لِكَىْ لَا يَكُونَ عَلَى ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ حَرَجٌۭ فِىٓ أَزْوَٰجِ أَدْعِيَآئِهِمْ إِذَا قَضَوْا۟ مِنْهُنَّ وَطَرًۭا ۚ وَكَانَ أَمْرُ ٱللَّهِ مَفْعُولًۭا ﴿٣٧﴾
"And [remember, O Muhammad], when you said to the one on whom Allah bestowed favor and you bestowed favor, "Keep your wife and fear Allah," while you concealed within yourself that which Allah is to disclose. And you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him. So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you in order that there not be upon the believers any discomfort concerning the wives of their adopted sons when they no longer have need of them. And ever is the command of Allah accomplished."
Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:37

Two hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī fix the context. Anas reports that the verse was revealed about Zaynab and Zayd (4787), and that the Prophet kept telling Zayd to fear God and keep his wife (7420). In the same report ʿĀʾishah remarks that if the Prophet had concealed anything of the Quran, he would have concealed this verse.

That remark answers the central accusation. The verse rebukes the Prophet for hiding something out of fear of what people would say, and it records that he urged Zayd to stay married. A man composing revelations to serve his desires would not publish a verse that criticises him and exposes the awkward detail he had tried to keep private. The verse's stated purpose is legal: to end the pre-Islamic rule that an adopted son's former wife was forbidden to the adoptive father, as if the adoption created a blood tie. The Quran makes the same point a few verses later:

مَّا كَانَ مُحَمَّدٌ أَبَآ أَحَدٍۢ مِّن رِّجَالِكُمْ وَلَٰكِن رَّسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَخَاتَمَ ٱلنَّبِيِّۦنَ ۗ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمًۭا ﴿٤٠﴾
"Muhammad is not the father of [any] one of your men, but [he is] the Messenger of Allah and last of the prophets. And ever is Allah, of all things, Knowing."
Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:40

Adoption in pre-Islamic Arabia transferred lineage, inheritance and name. The Quran abolished that legal fiction while keeping the duty of care for orphans and foster children, and the Prophet's marriage to Zaynab was the public demonstration that the old taboo no longer applied. Critics may disagree with the reform. They cannot fairly describe it as a pretext invented after the fact, because the verse that announces it is the one that rebukes him.

Later biographies contain a story in which the Prophet saw Zaynab unveiled and was struck by her beauty, and some critics build their case on it. The story has no sound chain, and scholars such as Ibn Kathīr declined to repeat it for that reason. Zaynab was the Prophet's cousin; he had known her all her life and had himself proposed her marriage to Zayd. A sudden infatuation fits the facts poorly.

Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy

Ṣafiyyah was the daughter of Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab, a chief of the Banū al-Naḍīr, and was among the captives taken at Khaybar in 628. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī records how the marriage was concluded:

أَعْتَقَ صَفِيَّةَ، وَجَعَلَ عِتْقَهَا صَدَاقَهَا
"He freed Ṣafiyyah and made her freedom her bridal gift."
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5086

In the warfare of the time, captured women became slaves, and the law of war in every neighbouring empire allowed it. The Prophet freed her, and the marriage followed her freedom, with her liberty itself as the dower. The sources report that she was offered the choice of returning to her people and chose to stay. Later reports record the other wives taunting her as the daughter of a Jew, and the Prophet telling her to answer that her father was Aaron, her uncle Moses and her husband Muhammad.

The marriage took place days after a battle in which her husband and relatives were killed, and modern readers find that difficult. The question is fair. The answer from the sources is that a woman of her rank, captured in war, faced either slavery in another household or the protection of marriage to the leader of the victors, and that the Prophet chose to free her and offer marriage. Her later life in Medina, as a respected wife and then a widow honoured by the caliphs, does not resemble the story the critics tell.

[ce_figure id="pexels-37985192"]Close-up view of a vibrant palm tree with ripe dates, capturing the essence of a sunny summer day.[/ce_figure]

Māriyah the Copt

Māriyah came to Medina as a gift from al-Muqawqis, the ruler of Egypt, in reply to the Prophet's letter. She bore him a son, Ibrāhīm, who died in infancy. Critics point out that the sources describe her as a concubine and not as one of the "mothers of the believers."

The status was a recognised one in the ancient world, including in the Hebrew Bible, where Abraham, Jacob, David and Solomon had concubines. Islamic law placed limits on it that the surrounding cultures did not: a concubine who bore her master a child became umm walad (mother of a child), could not be sold, and became free on his death, and the child was free and legitimate. Māriyah's son was the Prophet's acknowledged son, and the Prophet wept at his death. The scholars differ over whether she was formally freed in his lifetime, and both views are found in the classical literature.

Judged by the standards of its time, the relationship carried protections that slavery elsewhere lacked. Judged by modern standards, any form of slavery is objectionable, and the Islamic legal tradition itself encouraged manumission so strongly that freeing slaves became an expiation for many sins. The fair question is whether the Prophet's conduct moved his society toward or away from the abolition that later came, and the sources point toward.

[ce_figure id="pexels-36188877"]Close-up of an open Quran displaying Arabic calligraphy under warm lighting, conveying spirituality.[/ce_figure]

Reading the marriages as a whole

The Prophet was married to one woman, Khadījah, fifteen years his senior, for twenty-five years, until her death. Almost all of his later marriages took place in Medina during a decade of war, and most of the women were widows or divorcees. Several marriages sealed alliances with tribes, and several gave protection to women whose husbands had been killed. The Quran also told his wives that they were free to leave him if they preferred worldly comfort:

يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِىُّ قُل لِّأَزْوَٰجِكَ إِن كُنتُنَّ تُرِدْنَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَزِينَتَهَا فَتَعَالَيْنَ أُمَتِّعْكُنَّ وَأُسَرِّحْكُنَّ سَرَاحًۭا جَمِيلًۭا ﴿٢٨﴾
"O Prophet, say to your wives, "If you should desire the worldly life and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and give you a gracious release."
Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:28

None of this requires the reader to approve of every custom of seventh-century Arabia. It does require the critic to explain why a man supposedly driven by desire spent his youth in a single marriage to an older widow, published a verse that rebuked him over Zaynab, freed Ṣafiyyah before marrying her, and offered every wife the option of leaving. The charge of lust fits the summary. It fits the sources much less well.

articles.title: Does the Quran Contradict Itself? How to Test an Alleged Contradiction
articles.excerpt: Online lists claim hundreds of Quran contradictions. A contradiction has a strict definition, and testing a few famous examples shows how most of the lists are built.
articles.content:
The Quran makes a claim about itself that few scriptures make so directly: if it came from anyone other than God, its readers would find much contradiction in it. Critics have taken up the challenge, and lists of Quran contradictions now run to several hundred items. A list of that length looks overwhelming. Before answering any single item, it helps to ask what a contradiction is, because most of the entries fail that definition before their content is examined.

[ce_figure id="pexels-8522570"]Close-up of the Quran on a wooden stand, symbolizing Islamic spirituality.[/ce_figure]
أَفَلَا يَتَدَبَّرُونَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ ۚ وَلَوْ كَانَ مِنْ عِندِ غَيْرِ ٱللَّهِ لَوَجَدُوا۟ فِيهِ ٱخْتِلَٰفًۭا كَثِيرًۭا ﴿٨٢﴾
"Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? If it had been from [any] other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction."
Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:82

What counts as a contradiction

Two statements contradict each other when they cannot both be true in the same respect, about the same subject, at the same time. "The door is open" and "the door is closed" contradict only if they refer to the same door at the same moment. Most alleged contradictions in any long text, religious or secular, fail one of those conditions. Classical Muslim scholars developed a discipline, called mushkil al-Qurʾān (the problematic passages of the Quran), to examine precisely these cases, and they recognised the same tests a logician would apply.

Four questions settle most cases. Does each statement refer to the same subject? Is the same respect in view, for example literal or figurative, partial or total? Is the time or situation the same? And does the wider context of either verse qualify it? An alleged contradiction that fails any of the four is a difference, and differences are what a book addressing many situations over twenty-three years would be expected to contain.

Example one: does anyone bear another's burden?

The most widely cited case sets two kinds of verse against each other. The first states a principle of individual responsibility:

قُلْ أَغَيْرَ ٱللَّهِ أَبْغِى رَبًّۭا وَهُوَ رَبُّ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ ۚ وَلَا تَكْسِبُ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ إِلَّا عَلَيْهَا ۚ وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌۭ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ ۚ ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُم مَّرْجِعُكُمْ فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ ﴿١٦٤﴾
"Say, "Is it other than Allah I should desire as a lord while He is the Lord of all things? And every soul earns not [blame] except against itself, and no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you concerning that over which you used to differ.""
Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:164

The second says that those who lead others astray will carry some of the burdens of those they misled:

لِيَحْمِلُوٓا۟ أَوْزَارَهُمْ كَامِلَةًۭ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ ۙ وَمِنْ أَوْزَارِ ٱلَّذِينَ يُضِلُّونَهُم بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ ۗ أَلَا سَآءَ مَا يَزِرُونَ ﴿٢٥﴾
"That they may bear their own burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and some of the burdens of those whom they misguide without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is that which they bear."
Sūrat al-Naḥl 16:25

The two verses describe different burdens. The first denies that one person carries another's sins in place of that person, so that the misled are excused. The second says that the misleader carries the burden of his own act of misleading, which is a sin he committed, while the misled still answer for their own choices. Sūrat al-Naḥl makes this explicit: they bear "their own burdens in full" and some of the burdens of those they misguide. A teacher who corrupts a student is guilty of corrupting him; the student is still responsible for what he did. No court would find a contradiction there, and neither verse says that one person's guilt cancels another's.

Example two: is hell eternal?

Many verses describe the punishment of the wicked with the word khālidīn (abiding) and sometimes abadan (for ever). Critics set these against a verse in Sūrat Hūd:

فَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ شَقُوا۟ فَفِى ٱلنَّارِ لَهُمْ فِيهَا زَفِيرٌۭ وَشَهِيقٌ ﴿١٠٦﴾ ۞ وَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ سُعِدُوا۟ فَفِى ٱلْجَنَّةِ خَٰلِدِينَ فِيهَا مَا دَامَتِ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتُ وَٱلْأَرْضُ إِلَّا مَا شَآءَ رَبُّكَ ۖ عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍۢ ﴿١٠٨﴾
"As for those who were [destined to be] wretched, they will be in the Fire. For them therein is [violent] exhaling and inhaling. And as for those who were [destined to be] prosperous, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord should will - a bestowal uninterrupted."
Sūrat Hūd 11:106 to 108

The phrase "except what your Lord should will" appears for both the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise, and in the case of Paradise the verse immediately adds that the gift is uninterrupted. The exception therefore cannot mean that Paradise will end. Classical commentators read it as an assertion of God's sovereignty: the duration is God's decree and remains subject to His will, never a limit imposed on Him.

Some, especially in the case of the Fire, read the exception as referring to sinful believers who are eventually brought out. Either reading removes the contradiction, and the second also matches the many hadith on intercession. What the verse does not support is the critic's claim that the Quran asserts and denies eternal punishment in the same respect.

[ce_figure id="pexels-17543687"]Cozy vintage scene with candle, map, glasses, and magnifying glass.[/ce_figure]

Example three: different questions on the Day of Judgement

One verse says that all will be questioned:

فَوَرَبِّكَ لَنَسْـَٔلَنَّهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ ﴿٩٢﴾ عَمَّا كَانُوا۟ يَعْمَلُونَ ﴿٩٣﴾
"So by your Lord, We will surely question them all About what they used to do."
Sūrat al-Ḥijr 15:92 to 93

Another says that on that day no one will be asked about his sin:

فَيَوْمَئِذٍۢ لَّا يُسْـَٔلُ عَن ذَنۢبِهِۦٓ إِنسٌۭ وَلَا جَآنٌّۭ ﴿٣٩﴾
"Then on that Day none will be asked about his sin among men or jinn."
Sūrat al-Raḥmān 55:39

The answer lies in the stages the Quran describes. In one phase the guilty are questioned about their deeds to establish the record; in another the matter is settled and no inquiry is needed, because, as the next verse in Sūrat al-Raḥmān says, the criminals are known by their marks. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī preserves a report, in its commentary on Sūrat Fuṣṣilat, in which a man brought Ibn ʿAbbās a set of verses he thought contradictory and Ibn ʿAbbās explained them by the different stages of the Day. The report shows that the companions noticed such questions and answered them. It is early evidence that Muslims read the text carefully and did not hide its difficulties.

[ce_figure id="pexels-12591429"]Detailed view of the intricate dome design inside Humayun's Tomb, showcasing Islamic architecture in Delhi.[/ce_figure]

How the long lists are built

Testing a sample of the long lists reveals recurring patterns. Many entries set a verse about one group against a verse about another, such as believers against hypocrites. Many treat a figurative statement as literal, or a general rule as if it admitted no exceptions stated elsewhere. Many compare a Meccan verse addressed to a persecuted minority with a Medinan verse addressed to a governing community at war. Some depend on a mistranslation. A few concern genuine interpretive difficulties, and those deserve individual answers, which the classical commentaries and this site try to give.

The number of items on a list tells the reader how much effort went into compiling it. It does not tell the reader how many contradictions there are. A list of three hundred differences is not three hundred contradictions, and the honest way to evaluate it is to take its strongest five entries and test them against the four questions above.

The same standard for every text

The same method applies to any scripture, and critics who use it against the Quran should accept it for their own texts. Christian scholars resolve the differing accounts of Judas's death, or the two genealogies of Jesus, by asking whether the accounts describe the same thing in the same respect. That is a legitimate method. It is equally legitimate when applied to the Quran.

The Quran's challenge in 4:82 remains open. It invites reflection, which means reading each verse in its context, with its subject, time and purpose in view. Readers who do that with the most famous alleged contradictions find, as the classical scholars did, that the challenge has not been met.

articles.title: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Sun Setting in a Muddy Spring
articles.excerpt: Critics say Quran 18:86 teaches that the sun sets in a muddy spring and borrows from an Alexander legend. The grammar, the commentators and the dating tell a different story.
articles.content:
Sūrat al-Kahf tells of Dhul-Qarnayn, "the one with two horns," a righteous ruler who travels to the setting of the sun and then to its rising. At the western limit, the verse says, he found the sun setting in a spring of dark mud. Critics present the verse as a scientific error, since the sun sets in no spring, and as a borrowing from a Syriac legend about Alexander the Great. Both charges depend on how the verse is read, and the verse itself, together with fourteen centuries of commentary on it, settles more than the critics allow.

[ce_figure id="pexels-26952731"]A sunset reflecting over a tranquil lake, highlighting the serene beauty of nature.[/ce_figure]

The verse

وَيَسْـَٔلُونَكَ عَن ذِى ٱلْقَرْنَيْنِ ۖ قُلْ سَأَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْكُم مِّنْهُ ذِكْرًا ﴿٨٣﴾
"And they ask you, [O Muhammad], about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say, "I will recite to you about him a report.""
Sūrat al-Kahf 18:83
حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا بَلَغَ مَغْرِبَ ٱلشَّمْسِ وَجَدَهَا تَغْرُبُ فِى عَيْنٍ حَمِئَةٍۢ وَوَجَدَ عِندَهَا قَوْمًۭا ۗ قُلْنَا يَٰذَا ٱلْقَرْنَيْنِ إِمَّآ أَن تُعَذِّبَ وَإِمَّآ أَن تَتَّخِذَ فِيهِمْ حُسْنًۭا ﴿٨٦﴾
"Until, when he reached the setting of the sun, he found it [as if] setting in a spring of dark mud, and he found near it a people. Allah said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish [them] or else adopt among them [a way of] goodness.""
Sūrat al-Kahf 18:86

The key word is wajadahā: "he found it." The verse reports what Dhul-Qarnayn found when he reached the western limit of his journey, which is what he saw. A traveller standing on a western shore finds the sun setting in the sea; a traveller by a dark marsh or lake at sunset finds it setting into the water. The Quran describes the sight from his position, in the same way that English speakers still say that the sun rises and sets.

What the classical commentators said

The perspective reading was not invented to answer modern critics. Ibn Kathīr, writing in the fourteenth century, explained the phrase as meaning that Dhul-Qarnayn saw the sun as if it were setting in the ocean, adding that anyone who goes to the coast sees the same thing, while the sun never leaves the course fixed for it.

Al-Jalālayn, the most widely read short commentary, says that the setting in a spring is described as it appears to the eye, because the sun is in fact far larger than the earth. Muslim astronomers of the classical period, many of them devout, measured the circumference of the earth and the motions of the sun with considerable accuracy, and none of them read this verse as a description of the sun's physical resting place.

The Quran elsewhere describes the sun and the moon each moving in an orbit (21:33, 36:40), which a literal reading of 18:86 would contradict. A reader who takes one verse in isolation and ignores those statements has chosen the least coherent reading available.

The narrator objection

Critics reply that the narrator of the verse is God, who sees the sun as it is, so the verse cannot be a mere description of appearance. The objection misreads the grammar. God, the narrator, reports what Dhul-Qarnayn found. "He found it setting" is a statement about the traveller's experience, made accurately by the narrator. If a historian writes that Columbus found the sea calm on a given morning, the historian is describing what Columbus saw, and no one supposes that the historian believes the sea is always calm.

The verse continues in the same way. It says that at the rising of the sun Dhul-Qarnayn found a people for whom God had made no shelter from it (18:90). The sun did not rise on that people alone; it rose on them as he found them. Both verses describe the limits of a journey from the traveller's point of view.

[ce_figure id="pexels-39133256"]A view of a fiery sunset over the ocean, casting a warm glow and dramatic clouds.[/ce_figure]

The reading ḥāmiyah

The word translated "muddy," ḥamiʾah, has a well-known alternative among the canonical readings: ḥāmiyah, meaning hot or warm. The two readings agree in consonants and differ in vowels and in the hamzah. Commentators noted both and explained each in turn: a dark, muddy spring, or a hot spring, or both at once. The variant shows that the earliest Muslim readers were already discussing the phrase, and none of them drew the conclusion the critics draw.

The Alexander legend

The second charge is that the Quranic story depends on the Syriac "Alexander Legend," a Christian text in which Alexander travels to the ends of the earth, sees the sun enter a foul sea, and builds a gate against Gog and Magog. The parallels are real: the two journeys, the barrier and the peoples beyond it. Scholars who study the Syriac text have argued that it was composed in the early seventh century, around the time of the Byzantine emperor Heraclius's war with Persia, which would make it nearly contemporary with the Quranic passage.

Two observations follow. First, a near-contemporary text cannot easily be the source of the Quranic account if the story was already known to the Prophet's audience, as the opening verse implies: "they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn." The Quran answers a question about a figure its hearers already knew of. Second, where the two accounts overlap, the Quran's version differs in its emphasis.

The Syriac Alexander is a conqueror whose exploits serve imperial propaganda; the Quranic Dhul-Qarnayn is a just ruler who attributes his power to God, refuses payment for his barrier, and warns that it will crumble when God decrees. The Quran retells a story that circulated in its world and gives it a moral centre: power held in trust from God.

Retelling a known story with a corrected meaning is what the Quran says it does with earlier narratives. Whether one finds that persuasive depends on prior commitments about revelation. It is a different claim from the charge that the Quran copied an error, because the supposed error, the sun entering a body of water, appears in the Quran only as what a traveller saw.

[ce_figure id="pexels-15368077"]A aerial view of a town surrounded by mountains at sunrise, capturing the serene landscape and vibrant sky.[/ce_figure]

Who was Dhul-Qarnayn?

Muslim scholars have never agreed on his identity. Some early writers identified him with Alexander; many later scholars rejected that identification, since Alexander was a polytheist and the Quran presents Dhul-Qarnayn as a monotheist. Some modern Muslim writers identify him with Cyrus the Great of Persia, who is praised in the Hebrew Bible and associated in Daniel with a two-horned ram. The Quran leaves the name unstated, and its purpose in the passage does not depend on settling it.

A fair conclusion

Read with its grammar, its commentators and the rest of the Quran in view, 18:86 describes the setting sun as a traveller saw it at the western limit of his journey. The reading is old, it is grammatical, and it is consistent with the Quran's other statements about the sun. The Alexander parallels raise a legitimate question about how the Quran relates to the stories of its time, and that question deserves discussion. The charge that the verse teaches the sun sets in a muddy pool is the weakest part of the critic's case.

articles.title: Do Muslims Only Reject Hadith When They Are Embarrassing?
articles.excerpt: Critics say Muslims treat Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī as sound until a report embarrasses them. The stoned monkey and the fly in the drink show how the rules work.
articles.content:
A familiar charge runs like this: Muslims call Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī the most authentic book after the Quran, but when a report in it is embarrassing, such as monkeys stoning an adulteress or a fly dipped into a drink, they suddenly discover that it is weak, or misunderstood, or not really a hadith. Selective hadith use, critics conclude, shows that Muslims follow the sources only when convenient. The charge assumes that Muslim scholarship has no consistent rules for reading reports. It has, and two of the critics' favourite examples show them at work.

[ce_figure id="pexels-7967598"]A hand writing with a pen in a cozy library setting with a vintage typewriter.[/ce_figure]

What "authentic" means in hadith scholarship

When scholars call a report in al-Bukhārī ṣaḥīḥ (sound), they make a specific claim: that its chain of narrators is connected, that each narrator was upright and precise, and that the report is free of hidden defects and of contradiction with stronger evidence. The judgement concerns transmission. It says that a statement was reliably passed on from the person it is attributed to. It does not, by itself, say what kind of statement it is, whose words it records, or how it should be applied.

That distinction matters because al-Bukhārī's collection contains several kinds of material. Most of it records the words and actions of the Prophet. Some records the statements of companions and later figures, their opinions, their memories of pre-Islamic life, and their commentary. The book's full title describes it as a collection of the Prophet's affairs, his practice and his days, and al-Bukhārī included supporting reports in chapter headings and commentary that he did not hold to the same standard as his main narrations. Reading every line of the book as a prophetic command is a misreading of the book's structure.

The monkeys

رَأَيْتُ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ قِرْدَةً اجْتَمَعَ عَلَيْهَا قِرَدَةٌ قَدْ زَنَتْ، فَرَجَمُوهَا فَرَجَمْتُهَا مَعَهُمْ
"In the period before Islam I saw a she-monkey surrounded by a number of monkeys. They were stoning it because it had committed fornication, and I stoned it with them."
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3849

The report comes from ʿAmr ibn Maymūn, and its first words place it before Islam: "in the period before Islam I saw." It is his account of something he believed he witnessed in his youth, before he was a Muslim. The Prophet does not appear in it, says nothing in it, and approves nothing in it. Al-Bukhārī placed it in the chapter on the pre-Islamic period, among reports describing what life in that era was like.

Calling the report sound says that ʿAmr ibn Maymūn reliably told this story. Whether his interpretation of what he saw was correct is a separate question, and the scholars answered it plainly. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr rejected the idea that animals bear moral guilt, and Ibn Ḥajar, in his commentary, noted the objections and suggested that ʿAmr was describing what he took the animals' behaviour to mean. No Muslim legal school derives a ruling from the report. It is a memory of pre-Islamic Arabia, recorded with an honest chain, and no part of Islamic teaching depends on it.

[ce_figure id="pexels-32915594"]Hands writing traditional calligraphy with a pen on paper, showcasing cultural artistry in Baku.[/ce_figure]

The fly in the drink

إِذَا وَقَعَ الذُّبَابُ فِي شَرَابِ أَحَدِكُمْ فَلْيَغْمِسْهُ، ثُمَّ لِيَنْزِعْهُ، فَإِنَّ فِي إِحْدَى جَنَاحَيْهِ دَاءً وَالأُخْرَى شِفَاءً
"If a fly falls into the drink of one of you, let him dip it in, then take it out, for in one of its wings is a disease and in the other a cure."
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3320

This report is a saying of the Prophet with a sound chain, and Muslim scholars accept it as such. Here the critic's charge of selectivity fails from the other direction: the scholars did not reject it when it became awkward. What they discussed was its scope. The instruction concerns a drink into which a fly has already fallen, and it tells the drinker that the drink need not be thrown away. In a society where food and water were scarce, the instruction prevented waste, and the classical jurists derived from it the ruling that a fly does not make a liquid ritually impure.

The medical clause attracts the criticism. Some modern Muslim writers have pointed to research on antimicrobial substances produced by flies and by microorganisms they carry; others regard that research as too slender to bear the weight placed on it. A fair treatment does not need to settle the microbiology. The report gives a permission and a reason; Muslims who find the reason hard to evaluate remain free to discard a drink, since the instruction removes a prohibition and imposes no duty to drink. The critic who presents it as a command to drink contaminated liquid has added an element the text does not contain.

[ce_figure id="pexels-32046500"]A pile of books with blue covers on a white background, symbolizing education and knowledge.[/ce_figure]

When scholars do reject a report

Muslim scholars do reject reports, and they did so long before modern critics existed. The grounds are fixed and published: a broken chain, a narrator known for lying or poor memory, contradiction with the Quran or with better-established reports, or content that is impossible. These rules are applied to reports that flatter the Prophet as well as to those that critics find embarrassing. Ibn al-Jawzī's catalogue of fabricated reports is full of exaggerated praise of the Prophet, his family and his companions, rejected by the same standards that remove the story of Asmāʾ bint Marwān.

The selectivity charge would succeed if Muslim scholars rejected reports in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī for being embarrassing while keeping weak reports that suited them. The record shows something else. The scholars accepted sound reports even when they were awkward, as with the fly. They distinguished the Prophet's words from a companion's memory, as with the monkeys. And they rejected weak reports whatever their content.

The fair question

A critic is entitled to ask whether the hadith system as a whole is reliable. That is a serious question with a long scholarly literature, and this site discusses it in its articles on hadith authenticity. The narrower charge, that Muslims are inconsistent in using al-Bukhārī, fails on the two examples most often offered as proof. Both show the rules working as stated: a sound chain establishes that something was said, and the meaning and status of what was said is a second question, answered by reading the report.

articles.title: Was Jesus Crucified? What Quran 4:157 Claims and What History Can Show
articles.excerpt: Historians widely accept that Jesus was crucified, and the Quran says he was not killed or crucified. What each side claims, and where the real disagreement lies.
articles.content:
On one point most historians of early Christianity agree: the crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth under Pontius Pilate took place. On the same point the Quran is explicit: they did not kill him and did not crucify him. Christians see here the clearest case of the Quran contradicting history, and Muslim apologists have sometimes answered with theories that do more harm than good. This article sets out what Quran 4:157 claims, what historical method can and cannot establish, and why the disagreement is narrower than it first appears.

[ce_figure id="pexels-38446003"]Scenic view of historical wall and lush greenery in Jerusalem's Old City.[/ce_figure]

What the Quran says

وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا ٱلْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ فِيهِ لَفِى شَكٍّۢ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًۢا ﴿١٥٧﴾ بَل رَّفَعَهُ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ ۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًۭا ﴿١٥٨﴾
"And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain. Rather, Allah raised him to Himself. And ever is Allah Exalted in Might and Wise."
Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:157 to 158

The verse appears in a passage listing the faults of those who broke their covenant, and the specific fault here is a boast: "we killed the Messiah." The Quran denies the boast. It says they did not kill him and did not crucify him, that "it was made to appear so to them" (shubbiha lahum), that those who disagree about it are in doubt, and that God raised him to Himself.

The verse leaves much unstated. It does not say who, if anyone, was crucified in his place, and the phrase shubbiha lahum can be read as "it was made to seem so to them" with no substitute named. The substitution theories common in later Muslim literature, in which someone else was given Jesus's likeness, are interpretations of the verse, several of them drawn from reports of uncertain origin. The Quran's own claim is limited to three points: the boast was false, the matter appeared otherwise to observers, and God raised Jesus to Himself.

A theory to set aside

The South African speaker Ahmed Deedat popularised the view that Jesus was placed on the cross, fainted, was taken down alive and recovered. Christian critics attack this theory, and they are right to. It contradicts the historical consensus about what crucifixion did to the body, and it also contradicts the Quran, which says that they did not crucify him. A swoon on the cross is still a crucifixion. Muslims do not need the swoon theory, and the mainstream Muslim exegetical tradition never held it.

What historians can establish

The historical case for the crucifixion rests on the early Christian writings, especially Paul's letters, written within roughly two decades of the event; on the Gospel accounts; and on two non-Christian notices, in Josephus and Tacitus, which mention Jesus's execution under Pilate. Historians weigh these sources by ordinary criteria: early attestation, independent witnesses, and details that the early Christians would have had no reason to invent, such as the shame of a criminal's death.

By those criteria, historians conclude that the early Christian community believed and proclaimed that Jesus had been crucified, and that the Roman authorities executed a man they regarded as Jesus of Nazareth. Historical method can establish what observers believed and reported. It cannot establish whether God intervened to make an event appear other than it was, because the historian's tools have no access to divine action. That is a limit of method, acknowledged by historians themselves.

[ce_figure id="pexels-16746856"]Dramatic sunbeams penetrate through clouds, creating a captivating sky scene.[/ce_figure]

Where the disagreement lies

Set side by side, the claims overlap more than either side often admits. The Quran agrees that people believed Jesus had been killed; it says the matter "was made to appear so to them." The historian establishes that people believed Jesus had been killed and reported it. The Quran's denial concerns what happened in fact, behind the appearance; the historian's evidence concerns the appearance and the belief. A historian may judge the Quranic claim improbable on naturalistic assumptions, but the historical evidence and the Quranic claim are not two answers to the same question of method.

That is not a device for avoiding history. A Christian who believes the resurrection makes exactly the same move: historians can establish that the disciples believed they saw the risen Jesus, and the claim that God raised him lies beyond what the historian can confirm or deny. Both faiths assert that God acted at the end of Jesus's earthly mission. They disagree about what He did.

[ce_figure id="pexels-18717595"]The ancient Roman ruins of Jerash with its iconic colonnade and cityscape views.[/ce_figure]

What the Quran says about Jesus's death

Christian writers also point to verses that seem to speak of Jesus's death:

إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَىٰٓ إِنِّى مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَىَّ وَمُطَهِّرُكَ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ وَجَاعِلُ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوكَ فَوْقَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ ۖ ثُمَّ إِلَىَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَأَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ فِيمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ ﴿٥٥﴾
"[Mention] when Allah said, "O Jesus, indeed I will take you and raise you to Myself and purify you from those who disbelieve and make those who follow you [in submission to Allah alone] superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that in which you used to differ."
Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:55
وَٱلسَّلَٰمُ عَلَىَّ يَوْمَ وُلِدتُّ وَيَوْمَ أَمُوتُ وَيَوْمَ أُبْعَثُ حَيًّۭا ﴿٣٣﴾
"And peace is on me the day I was born and the day I will die and the day I am raised alive.""
Sūrat Maryam 19:33

The verb in 3:55, mutawaffīka, means "taking you in full," and the Quran uses the same root for sleep (6:60, 39:42) as well as for death. Most classical commentators read it as God taking Jesus up, body and soul, and linked it to the raising mentioned in 4:158. In 19:33, Jesus speaks of the day he will die as an event still to come, which fits the Muslim belief that he will return and die a natural death. Christians read these verses differently, and the Quran's wording permits discussion. What it does not permit is the conclusion that it affirms the crucifixion, since 4:157 denies it in plain terms.

The theological core

Behind the historical argument lies the theological one. For Christianity the crucifixion is the means of atonement, and without it the faith loses its centre. The Quran rejects the need for that atonement: each soul bears its own burden, God forgives those who repent, and no one dies for another's sin (6:164). The denial of the crucifixion is therefore part of a coherent alternative account of how human beings are reconciled to God.

Readers weighing the two faiths should see the question in those terms. The historical record shows what the first Christians believed. Whether God allowed His Messiah to die on a cross, or raised him before the end the observers thought they saw, is a question about God's ways with His prophets, and each tradition answers it from its own scripture. The Quran's answer is consistent with its whole teaching about God, sin and forgiveness.
